content: Ear pain, also known as otalgia, can either originate from the ear itself (primary otalgia) or from structures outside the ear (secondary otalgia). Determining the exact cause of ear pain can be challenging due to the complex innervation of the ear. Sensory input to the middle ear, external auditory canal, auricle, and peri-auricular tissues is provided by branches of the fifth (trigeminal), seventh (facial), ninth (glossopharyngeal), and tenth (vagus) cranial nerves, as well as cervical nerves C1, C2, and C3. Irritation of any of these nerves can result in otalgia. Additionally, otalgia can sometimes be a referred pain from other conditions, such as myocardial ischemia (angina equivalent), due to the shared sensory innervation of the vagus nerve. Intermittent ear pain is more commonly associated with musculoskeletal conditions, such as temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction or other myofascial pain syndromes. Otalgia is classified into two categories: primary otalgia, which originates from the ear, and secondary otalgia, which originates from structures outside the ear. If the ear examination reveals abnormalities, the pain is likely primary otalgia. Conversely, if the ear examination is normal, the pain is likely secondary otalgia. A thorough examination should include inspection of the nasal cavity, oral cavity, neck, and potentially the larynx to identify the source of the pain. Life-Threatening Causes of Otalgia While otalgia itself is not inherently life-threatening, certain characteristics may indicate a more serious underlying condition. Patients aged 50 years or older, those with coronary artery disease, diabetes, or immunocompromised states, as well as individuals who smoke, consume alcohol, or experience unintentional weight loss, are at higher risk for serious diagnoses. Otalgia may be the initial symptom of the following conditions: Temporal arteritis Myocardial infarction Thoracic aneurysms Subdural hematoma Lung cancer Central line placement complications Carotid artery aneurysm Pott puffy tumor Malignant neoplasms Common Causes of Otalgia Primary Otalgia (originating from the ear): Otitis media Otitis externa Barotrauma Eustachian tube dysfunction Presence of a foreign object in the ear Cellulitis of the auricle Cholesteatoma Secondary Otalgia (originating outside the ear): Bell’s palsy Carotidynia Cervical adenopathy Cervical spine arthritis Cricoarytenoid arthritis Dental infections Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) Head and neck tumors Temporomandibular joint syndrome Myofascial pain syndromes Neuralgias (trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, geniculate, sphenopalatine) Oral aphthous ulcers Pharyngitis or tonsillitis Salivary gland disorders Sinusitis Thyroiditis Diagnosis The diagnostic approach to ear pain is guided by algorithms, such as those provided by the American Family Physician (AFP) guidelines from 2008. These algorithms help clinicians systematically evaluate the potential causes of otalgia based on clinical findings and patient history. Treatment Treatment strategies for ear pain are also outlined in algorithms, such as those from the American Family Physician guidelines. These algorithms provide evidence-based recommendations for managing both primary and secondary otalgia, tailored to the underlying cause of the pain.
